RagShortTexts: Counterweight trebuchets revolutionized sieges, launching massive boulders using box ballast.

Variants.Content: By the mid-thirteenth century the counterweight trebuchet had outclassed the older traction engines, which depended on teams of men hauling a sling. The machine used a long pivoted beam with a heavy box of earth or scrap metal on its short arm, and the falling weight swung the long arm around to launch a dressed masonry ball of about 300 pounds. Because gravity drew the weight down steadily, its power was far more consistent than human effort, and it sent stones on flatter, heavier trajectories against thick curtain walls. Castle builders answered by raising sloped taluses at the foot of their walls, so that stones would glance off instead of crushing the masonry above.

Castles now needed massive sloping taluses at their base to turn aside boulders that plunged from above. A master siege engineer and his timber-wrights could be worth more than fifty heavy cavalry during a campaign, since one trebuchet could bring down a wall that would otherwise hold off a season of assaults. Rival lords who lacked such men learned that their castles were no longer safe.

Nothing chills the blood like the groaning ratchet of a siege engine's windlass. When a three-hundred-pound rock strikes the parapet, flying splinters of stone butcher men faster than any volley of arrows. Crouching behind the merlons, you hear each shot land and wait for the next, counting the seconds until the ground shudders again.
